source.title: SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics
source.authors: Emmanuel Abbe; Enric Boix-Adserà; Theodor Misiakiewicz

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes SGD learning on synthetic low-dimensional regression functions and reports squared population-risk results. It does not test the stated classification-error versions or their CIFAR benchmarks, local minima, depth, initialization comparisons, learning-rate stability thresholds, or batch-normalization comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports synthetic regression learning and alignment outcomes, but these do not measure the classification behavior named in the claim versions. Results it cites from other work are not extracted as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study's own results concern population squared risk and support alignment for synthetic regression. They do not test any listed version. Figure 7 changes depth, activation and residual architecture together, without the plain batch-normalized convolutional comparison in V3. Appendix A mentions nonmonotonic loss but measures neither sharpness nor a stability threshold required by V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conjecture that leap complexity governs online-SGD learning time, prove restricted Gaussian polynomial cases using layerwise training and projection, and provide simulations with vanilla SGD. Removing the training modifications and extending the proof to general targets remain future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses online SGD for squared-loss regression on synthetic isotropic data, with layerwise training and projected first-layer updates in its formal analysis. The experiments also include vanilla SGD, but do not evaluate the classification-error claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The formal guarantees depend on target-function structure, the layerwise training schedule, projected first-layer updates, activation assumptions, and step counts. Early stopping changes the reported approximation outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: Modified layerwise online SGD learns specified Gaussian polynomial regression targets to population risk at most ε; stopping first-layer training early leaves a large approximation error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For restricted low-dimensional polynomial targets, modified online SGD has learning complexity governed by leap complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 7 reports faster, better fitting by a five-layer ReLU fully connected ResNet than by a two-layer sigmoid network on Gaussian polynomial regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and activation choices can affect fitting after relevant input coordinates have been identified.

record.problems: The formal guarantees apply to restricted synthetic regression targets and modified SGD with layerwise training and projection. The paper notes that it does not prove the general conjecture for arbitrary functions and leaves removing these training modifications for future work. Several numerical outcomes are shown in figures rather than given as precise values.
record.rows_left_out: No figure-only risk trajectories were extracted: those plots report synthetic regression learning curves and do not measure any version’s classification-error outcome. Results attributed to cited prior work were excluded.

untested.parts: Training classification error in convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including corrupted labels, and its dependence on size, stopping and regularization.
Spurious local-minimum frequencies in ReLU teacher-student networks and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Depth degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, matched identity-shortcut comparisons, and the special initialization and Fixup results.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient preservation, initialization comparisons, and trainable depth.
Recovery above the initial stability limit, curvature reduction, sharpness tracking the threshold, and divergence relative to that threshold.
Matched batch-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The omitted numerical trajectories are declared in rows_left_out and do not warrant verdicts on the listed versions. Nonmonotonic loss alone does not establish edge-of-stability behavior.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error; CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; corrupted or random labels; convolutional networks; SGD or Adam comparisons; model size and training duration effects.
Teacher-student ReLU networks; spurious local minima rates; varying teacher and student widths.
Plain versus residual depth comparisons; batch-normalized convolutional networks; ImageNet and CIFAR-10; special deep tanh initialization; Fixup.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons; Gaussian versus orthogonal weights; deep tanh and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature changes, edge-of-stability behavior, and divergence comparisons.
Batch-normalization comparisons on MNIST, CIFAR-10, or ImageNet, and Fixup comparisons without normalization.

rows.check: The low population-risk guarantee is correctly extracted, but it cannot establish any listed version's effect. It is a theorem for modified layerwise projected SGD, rather than an empirical classification result.

rows.check: The population-risk guarantee does not measure any listed version. Its activation condition should specify existence of a suitable activation; the guarantee does not cover every activation satisfying Assumption 1.

rows.note: This early-stopping result concerns approximation of a synthetic regression target; it does not measure classification error.
rows.check: The lower bound is misread: Corollary 1(b) gives ≥ 1 − log(d)/d^D, not ≥ 1 − log(d)/M. The nearby M belongs to the optimization domain a ∈ R^M. This is an early-stopping approximation lower bound, unrelated to the listed classification-error or local-minimum claims.
